import { Code } from '@astrojs/starlight/components'
import serve from '../../../../snippets/serve.ts?raw'
import compose from '../../../../snippets/compose-routes.ts?raw'
import tenants from '../../../../snippets/tenants.ts?raw'
import notify from '../../../../snippets/notify.ts?raw'

`@familiar-ai/core/http` turns a Familiar into a [Hono](https://hono.dev) app: JSON commands plus one server-sent event stream at `/events`. Any runtime with the Fetch API can serve it.

## Choose routes

`createHttpApi` takes an `authenticate` function and the `routes` to serve. It serves nothing you don't choose: every route you leave out answers 404, and with no event sources there is no `/events`.

<Code code={serve} lang="ts" title="api.ts" />

Mount it under any path, such as `new Hono().route('/api', createApi(familiar))`, and give your frontend its type, `Api`. The client then offers exactly the commands whose routes you serve.

`routes` groups operations the way the client groups its commands:

| Group          | Operations                                                                 |
| -------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `conversation` | `send`, `history`, `abort`, `modelOptions`, `setModel`, `setThinkingLevel` |
| `account`      | `state`, `signIn`, `answerSignIn`, `cancelSignIn`, `signOut`               |
| `memory`       | `health`, `revise`, `retire`, `setPinned`                                  |
| `schedules`    | `cancel`                                                                   |
| `push`         | `key`, `subscribe`, `unsubscribe`                                          |
| `connections`  | `list`, `setSecret`, `deleteSecret`                                        |
| `mcp`          | `add`, `remove`, `reconnect`                                               |
| `events`       | `conversation`, `memory`, `episodes`, `schedules`, `account`               |

Each one is `true`, for everyone `authenticate` accepts, or your own check, `(author, request) => boolean | Promise<boolean>`. Familiar asks the check on every request to that route, after authentication and the body limit, and answers 403 unless it returns `true`, before the route reads anything or changes anything. Each check covers only its own operation: `signIn` and `cancelSignIn` share a path but each asks its own. A name that isn't an operation is a type error, and throws when Familiar starts.

`events` chooses what `/events` streams. Each source is checked once, when a stream connects: revoking someone's access applies from their next connection, not to a stream they already have open. A stream every chosen source refuses answers 403. Account routes don't stream the account: its sign-in page and code arrive only through `events.account`, so keep that source to the people who sign in. `events: true` streams every source.

`routes: true` serves every route and every event source, including any that Familiar adds later, to everyone `authenticate` accepts. Use it only when everyone who can reach the API is the Familiar's owner. The daemon does, because only its owner can reach it. Pass `push` as well if your host offers Web Push. Without it, the `/push` routes answer 404 so clients can tell notifications aren't available. See [Notifications](#notifications).

`authenticate` receives each request and returns the person making it as `{ id, name }`, or `undefined` to answer 401. The result becomes the author of any message that request sends. Request bodies can't choose their own author.

Request bodies are limited to `maxBodySize` bytes, by default `DEFAULT_MAX_BODY_SIZE` (1 MiB), and larger ones answer 413. Route groups you mount yourself don't get this limit, so add Hono's `bodyLimit` in front of them. Familiar checks field bounds such as `MESSAGE_LIMITS` itself, for every caller.

## A shared conversation is shared

Everyone who can send to a Familiar is in one conversation. They all read its history, and the model reads all of it too, so anything said, any tool's result and anything the model recalls from memory can reach every participant in a reply. Leaving memory out of `events` keeps the memory document off the stream, but it doesn't make memory private: the model can repeat what it remembers. Familiar doesn't promise per-message secrecy. Give people who mustn't share information [separate Familiars](#one-familiar-per-tenant).

## Identity is not permission

Familiar records who said what and shows the model each author. It doesn't decide who may do what. Your host must:

- authenticate every request, including the event stream
- decide who may use each route, with `routes`
- choose each Familiar's audience: who may send to it, and so share it
- choose each Familiar's tools, with `plugins` and its MCP servers
- choose who receives each notification, and store and authorize push subscriptions
- decide which MCP transports, destinations and commands it allows

Every tool installed on a Familiar is available to everyone who chats with it, just as its conversation is. Familiar has no per-person tool permissions. Where a tool's data or actions need narrower rules, such as who may change a task, the tool enforces them, or the app API behind it does, using `api.author`. That is the person the call runs for, from the stored input that started it, never from the tool's arguments: the author of the message, or the creator of a scheduled run. It's `undefined` for Familiar's own memory upkeep, and for a message an older version stored with only a name.

Nested calls, and calls rerun after a crash, keep the author of the input that started them, and a message queued while a call runs can't take its place. Familiar stores who started each call, never a permission, so your app's current rules apply when a tool checks them:

```ts
execute: async ({ taskId }, { author }) => {
  // Your API checks, as it runs, whether this person may change the task.
  if (!author) {
    return {
      output: [{ type: 'text', text: 'Only a person can do this.' }],
      isError: true,
    }
  }
  return updateTask(taskId, { as: author.id })
}
```

`api.author` is for native tools made with `defineTool`. An MCP server's tools receive only their arguments, so an MCP server can't tell who asked.

Schedules are shared controls, like the conversation: anyone who chats with a Familiar can see and cancel any of its schedules, so Alice can cancel Bob's reminder. That's the group's contract, not a missing check. A scheduled run's tools see the schedule's creator as `api.author`. Give people who mustn't share tools or schedules separate Familiars.

Native tools are code you install, trusted like any other dependency. They run in your process with its privileges. Familiar doesn't sandbox them. The host's `fetch` and `authorizedFetch`'s declarations limit where a well-behaved tool sends requests and secrets, whatever the model asks for, not what the tool's own code can do.

## One Familiar per tenant

When your app has separate audiences, such as teams, households or customers, open one Familiar for each, over that audience's own storage. Choose it from the authenticated session, never from anything the request says. Each Familiar then has its own conversation, memory, tools, schedules and secrets:

<Code code={tenants} lang="ts" title="tenants.ts" />

Mount `host.fetch` under your API path, for example with Hono's `app.mount('/api', host.fetch)`. Only one live Familiar may own a storage, so a host that runs several processes routes each tenant to one of them, as a Durable Object does on [Cloudflare](/familiar/build/cloudflare/).

## Notifications

Familiar's `notify` says what to show and, for a scheduled run, which schedule it was and who created it. It never chooses recipients. This tenant's `notify` delivers through the app's own preferences and notifications, without Familiar's push routes:

<Code code={notify} lang="ts" title="notify.ts" />

The creator is attribution, not a recipient. Familiar's `/push` routes are optional, for hosts that want browser Web Push. A `PushHost` stores subscriptions and decides what each person may change. Its `subscribe` and `unsubscribe` receive the subscription and the authenticated `Author`. Store each subscription with its subscriber's `id`, and let unsubscribing remove only that person's own: an endpoint is not proof of whose browser it is. See [Notifications](/familiar/reference/core/#notifications) for the types.

## What the daemon does for itself

These protections are the installed daemon's own, for a host that only its owner reaches. `createHttpApi` doesn't apply them to your host, so choose your own.

The daemon authenticates every request as its owner, with the stable ID `owner`, serves every route and relies on the network for access. It listens on loopback, is published only on the owner's tailnet and refuses requests whose `Host` isn't an IP address, `localhost` or a `.ts.net` name.

Because the browser sends the network along with every request, the daemon also uses Hono's `csrf` middleware against cross-site requests. It refuses a browser's form or bodyless `POST` unless `Sec-Fetch-Site` is `same-origin` or `Origin` names the `Host` the request was sent to. That still accepts the daemon's own page through Tailscale Serve and through Vite's proxy. A JSON `POST` from another site needs a CORS preflight, which the daemon never grants, so a browser doesn't send it. Requests with neither header, such as from the CLI or `curl`, aren't from a browser and pass. If your host authenticates browsers with cookies or other ambient credentials, add the same protection, because `createHttpApi` doesn't.

The daemon's own web UI also refuses to be shown inside another site's page, with `Content-Security-Policy: frame-ancestors 'none'` and `X-Frame-Options: DENY`. Those headers are the daemon's, not `createHttpApi`'s: a host that embeds Familiar in its own pages, or in a frame, sets its own framing policy.

The daemon's Web Push stores each subscription with the authenticated subscriber who added it, and subscribing or unsubscribing changes only that subscriber's entries. The daemon authenticates every request as `owner`, so all of its devices share one subscriber. A host that authenticates separate people receives each person's `Author` and must enforce the same scoping in its `PushHost` implementation. It also gives each delivery a 30-second socket inactivity timeout, web-push's `timeout`, so a push service that stops answering can't hold up a scheduled run. That limits silence, not a delivery's total time or the size of its response. A failed delivery is reported and doesn't stop other devices getting theirs.

The daemon gives plugins a `fetch` that refuses every address that isn't public unicast, on each connection and every redirect. Its web UI renders replies with Streamdown, which sanitises their HTML, and draws Mermaid diagrams in strict mode. Those reduce what a reply can do in the page, but they aren't a verified guarantee against script injection. Anyone who can reach the daemon can add MCP servers, including local commands that run as the daemon's user.

## Compose routes yourself

To mount Familiar's routes beside your own or behind your own middleware, compose the route factories instead. Each one is a Hono app you mount at its standard path, built from the same operations `routes` names, such as `memoryOperations(familiar.memory).health`:

| Factory              | Mount at       | Commands                                    |
| -------------------- | -------------- | ------------------------------------------- |
| `conversationRoutes` | `/`            | send messages, abort, read history          |
| `modelRoutes`        | `/model`       | list, switch model and reasoning level      |
| `memoryRoutes`       | `/memory`      | revise, retire and pin facts; memory health |
| `scheduleRoutes`     | `/schedules`   | cancel a schedule                           |
| `accountRoutes`      | `/account`     | sign in, answer, cancel, sign out           |
| `pushRoutes`         | `/push`        | VAPID key, subscribe, unsubscribe           |
| `connectionRoutes`   | `/connections` | list connections, set and delete secrets    |
| `mcpRoutes`          | `/mcp`         | add, remove and reconnect MCP servers       |
| `eventRoutes`        | `/`            | the `/events` stream                        |

`conversationRoutes` and `pushRoutes` take a function that returns the author for a request. This host exposes the conversation plus memory, to people trusted with memory:

<Code code={compose} lang="ts" title="host.ts" />

## Choose event sources

The event stream is a separate choice from the commands. `routes.events`, and `eventRoutes` when you compose, open only the sources you choose:

- `conversation` sends the view and each commit's changes.
- `memory`, `episodes` and `schedules` each send a document and its changes.
- `account` sends the sign-in state. Pass `null` to send `null` once, telling clients the host manages credentials itself.

Mounting `memoryRoutes` doesn't add memory to the stream, and streaming memory doesn't allow memory commands.

The [HTTP API reference](/familiar/reference/http/) lists every route and event.
